The first thing my father got wrong about our town was the smell. He had built the railway station down to the wire basket beside the ticket window, and the wire basket contained three twists of paper, each no bigger than a flea. But the whole station smelled of the glue he used on it. The real one smelled of floor wax, wet coats, and the orange my mother always peeled on the platform, digging her thumbnail in to get the first piece started.

I mentioned this when I was nine. My father held out a paintbrush.

“Show me how to paint a smell.”

I took this as a genuine assignment and spent most of Saturday rubbing orange peel on the station roof. For years afterward, one corner of the roof was darker than the rest. Visitors assumed it was water damage, skillfully rendered. My father accepted their compliments.

The town occupied two doors laid flat across four trestles in our basement. You had to duck beneath the doors and come up through a hole to reach the municipal swimming pool. This meant that anybody repairing the diving board appeared, from the perspective of the railway passengers, to be an enormous disembodied head rising behind the Methodist church. My mother liked to go down there when my father had company and slowly emerge, eating an apple.

He had rules. Nothing went into the town until he had seen it himself. No building could be included merely because it would be interesting to make. No person could appear twice, which became a problem when the postman, already permanently stationed outside the bakery, was elected mayor. My father left the mayor’s chair empty. He said the man still had his rounds.

By the time I left home, the model was sixteen years out of date. The cinema was showing a picture nobody remembered. Our old blue car stood outside a house we had sold. In actual life the council had filled in the swimming pool after a crack opened along its bottom and proved too expensive to fix. In the basement, a girl in a yellow bathing cap was forever deciding whether to jump.

My father died in February, when the ground was too hard for my mother to do much in the garden and the days were too short for her to want to do much else. I stayed for a fortnight. We cleared his wardrobe, canceled his appointments, and ate food brought by women who had all somehow agreed that what had happened called for grated cheese. Neither of us mentioned the town until the night before I was due to leave.

“I’d like my basement back,” she said.

I had imagined the model going to a museum. It turned out that museums had basements of their own, already full of things people had imagined going to museums. The library offered to take the station, but only if we could put it in a case. The school wanted the whole town until somebody measured the classroom door. Finally my mother put a notice in the paper: MODEL TOWN TO BE DISMANTLED. RESIDENTS MAY COLLECT THEIR PREMISES SATURDAY, TEN TO FOUR.

I extended my stay. I wanted to see who came.

The baker came first. He was a young man who had bought the business the previous summer and had never met my father. He turned the little building over and discovered, penciled underneath, the date of its completion and the words *rear gutter doubtful*. He promised to check. Two sisters arrived for the same house and, after a brief conference on the stairs, decided that the elder would keep it and the younger would have the cinema, where she had once been sick into the elder’s handbag.

All morning people carried buildings up into the daylight. Empty rectangles of green paint appeared where houses had stood. A man in a good suit asked for the bus shelter. He had waited there every evening for three years while courting his wife, who lived in the next town. My mother wrapped it in a square of tissue as carefully as if it were a piece of wedding cake.

At half past three, a woman I didn’t know came down the steps sideways, favoring one knee. She stood for a long time beside the pool.

“I worked the desk there,” she said. “Seventeen summers. People think it was a nice cool job, but that little office was an oven.”

She pointed out the open window my father had given the office, and the matchstick propping it up.

“That’s right,” she said, pleased. “Otherwise it fell on your fingers.”

We couldn’t lift the pool. It had been set into the door itself, a shallow rectangle carved out with a chisel and painted an improbable Mediterranean blue. I offered her the girl on the diving board. Instead she chose the office window, which came away easily, matchstick and all. She put it in the coin compartment of her purse.

By four there was hardly anything left. My mother took the Methodist church, not out of any religious feeling but because, she said, she had always enjoyed the view from behind it. I took the station. We unscrewed the trestles and leaned the doors against the wall. Underneath them the concrete floor was clean and pale except for four little rust rings and one ancient apple sticker.

The station sits on my kitchen shelf now, between the cookbooks and a cup of foreign coins. Last winter my daughter asked about the dark patch on the roof. I told her about her grandfather, his rules, and the Saturday I spent trying to paint a smell. She listened with the serious attention children reserve for accounts of adults doing something foolish.

“Did it work?” she asked.

I took down the station. Quite solemnly, we put our noses to the roof. There was dust, certainly, and the dry, faint sweetness of old cardboard. My daughter shook her head. But I could smell that orange.
